failure_matrix_paid_path.how: A true mid-run network cut needs a change to the host's /etc/hosts or firewall, which this worker will not make. The same failure mode was produced directly: one variant's evaluation child was killed 35 seconds into a live comparison, which is exactly what the product sees when the child dies after the run has started. Techtree does not parse provider HTTP status, so a mid-run provider or network failure reaches the user through this same code path.

failure_matrix_paid_path.why_not: Not honestly triggerable in a live journey. The product refuses on both sides before it can arise: if the evaluation child exits non-zero the pair fails first with variant_execution_failed, which was triggered; if it exits zero with nothing usable, the next stage refuses with variant_output_incomplete. Reaching episode_count_mismatch would mean deleting lines from a finished traces.jsonl by hand, which tests the receipt builder rather than the journey. Recorded as not triggerable rather than faked.

There is nothing to trigger. In v0.1 the Campaign's maximum_usd is declared and nothing more: no code path meters spend, compares it against the ceiling, or aborts. Only the token ceilings are handed to the engine. The CLI says this plainly on the review surface — 'nothing here works out what the run will come to first, and nothing stops it if it goes past' — and decision 0025 forbids any wording that would suggest a meter. Recorded as not triggerable, which is the honest answer, rather than staged.

journey.argv_difference: A file:// URL points at the local candidate repository instead of github.com/regents-ai/techtree-hermes, because that repository is not public before Gate 2. The --ref flag and the 40-character commit are exactly the pinned bootstrap argv.

open_findings.summary: techtree climb start tells every user, at the moment they approve spending their own money, that the run uses the development fake executor and no model will be called. The flag is a hardcoded literal. The run then calls models and bills them. run status and run result are correct; only the start path is wrong.

The one guided revision the introduction allows was consumed by a narrative guard that reads the hyphen in 'modulo-97' as a signed delta. The revision itself was fine. A rejection spends the turn with no recourse.

The Skill scanner blocks the ordinary sentence 'that token: no reasoning' as a credential assignment. Every Skill written for this Climb is about returning a token, so this is a likely everyday refusal, not a corner case.
A killed worker orphans its evaluation children, which keep spending, and leaves subject containers running. No reconciliation command exists.
The worker sanitizer redacts the word 'the', so a signed-out user reads 'no credential: [redacted] Prime CLI configuration'.
The README says doctor --for-evaluation checks the credential and image. It does not; --climb does.
The published install argv lands on Python 3.14 on a machine whose default is 3.14, and the user's first doctor fails.
ReleaseCore integrity is not checked on the run path. A tampered ReleaseCore is caught only by explicitly running techtree release verify.

Several typed errors carry no machine-readable repair action: techtree_home_unusable, starter_skill_source_refused, starter_skill_digest_mismatch. The human messages are honest and the repairs exist as flags; only the next_actions list is empty.

findings.summary: The one guided revision was destroyed a second time. The host completion spent its whole 32,768-token ceiling on reasoning, returned no content, billed USD 0.1589, and the product counted the attempt as used. The typed code is host_llm_unavailable, which is untrue: the host answered and charged for it.
The wheel checksum sidecar in dist/ still names the previous wheel's digest. Local artifact today, but it is the thing whose output becomes half the published release coordinate.
